body_markdown:
Ben had fixed the fuel leak, but fumes filled the engine bay. Without options, he pressed the ignition button and all hell broke loose. A fiery orange flash erupted from the engine cover, the report shaking the bones of occupants and vessel alike. Gale-force winds had whipped the sea into angry sheets of pelting spindrift, and 40-foot waves tossed the tiny craft as if it were a toy. Without power and unable to maneuver into the waves, he knew the next one could crush a window and they would go down. Hove to in a hurricane for seven days, Ben and Elinore Carlin had practiced the abandon ship drill a thousand times: “You shout ‘Out!’ I get out and wait. You follow and grab the gear…”


After a 2000-mile crossing of the Atlantic in the most unlikely of vessels, a 1942 Ford General Purpose Amphibian, or GPA, they had reached the Azores archipelago, between Fayal and Madeira. There had been no time for fear; only instinct and luck could keep them alive. Thoughts raced through his head. Could this be the end… or was he too damn ornery to die?


## The Backstory


Copenhagen, 1951


Guildford Grammar School


I came across Ben Carlin’s tale a few years ago, and the thought of “driving” across oceans in a vehicle discontinued due to its inability to stay afloat was so implausible I needed to know more. What happened to the Carlins? Did the vehicle survive? If so, where is it now? What drives a person to chase such a suicidal idea?


I sourced several books on the subject detailing the build, love affairs and flings, binge drinking with dignitaries and dregs, and a man obsessed. To learn more, we’re slipping into the jump seat for a highlight reel of this decade-long journey. First, however, we must examine the gray matter of a man crazy enough to sail a 5000-pound boat anchor across oceans.


Australian explorer Ben Carlin and his wife Elinore posing together in 1955.


Evening Standard/Hulton Archive/Getty Images


## Western Australia


Carlin’s mother died when he was four, and his father shipped him to a boarding school in Perth. Upon graduating he landed a job as a roughneck in the mine fields. With an alley-cat attitude, Ben was a born scrapper with a proclivity for taking on challenges and beating down challengers. Bars, booze, brothels, and brawls became his modus operandi.


Looking at a dead-end future, he earned a mining degree and signed on with a British company in China. As World War II swept the planet, Carlin longed to demonstrate his mettle and enlisted in the Indian Army. But rather than being issued a rifle, he found himself overseeing the construction of latrines. Badass Major Carlin had been reduced to the ranks of toilet digger. When the war ended, he was tasked with inspecting deserted installations in West Bengal. It was here that Ben stumbled across an odd-looking vehicle among the rows of rusting equipment. The cabin resembled a Willys MB, but with a boat hull wrapped around it and a propeller jutting out the back.


1943 Willys GPA


Chris Collard


“One could go around the world in one of these things,” he told a coworker. The reply was curt: “Impossible.” Not one to let a crazy idea dissolve for the fact that it was crazy, Carlin became obsessed with the prospect.


As boredom and gin consumed his life, instead of returning to Perth, he requested passage to the U.S., where he might find a surplus Ford GPA like the one he’d seen. With war in the rearview mirror, the world yearned to read about anything but front lines and casualties. Certainly, the media would take interest in his scheme, and a manufacturer would pony up cash. But he needed a partner. This merited a stop in China to pitch the idea to Elinore, the vivacious Boston brunette with whom he’d had a torrid relationship in India. It was a hard sell, though, and Ben landed in the States alone.


## On the Hunt


After researching land routes and ocean currents, he drafted a proposal. He would sail to Africa via the Azores, drive up the coast to Europe, then east toward Asia. He met no takers while presenting the plan to Willys-Overland, Ford, and any manufacturer that would listen. Carlin was on his own.


> *If you don’t bet you don’t win—if you stand to win you must also stand to lose.*
>
>
> *—Ben*


He paid a visit to the War Assets Administration in Washington, D.C., which was tasked with disposing of surplus military equipment and property. There he pored through catalogs, bent the ears of officials, and talked his way into a government auction. After months on the hunt, he slapped down $901 and became the owner of a well-used Seep, or Sea Jeep.


Stellantis


## Unlikely Mariner


Worth noting here is that the GPA was one of the worst maritime concepts ever contrived, often referred to as a floating coffin. It was heavy, difficult to maneuver on land and worse in water, and routinely sank in the lightest of seas.


**Ford GPA Specifications**


- **Production years:** 1942–43
- **Units produced:** 12,778
- **Weight:** 2450 lb / 3,550 lb GVW
- **Engine:** 134-cu-in flathead four-cylinder
- **Output:** 60 hp; 105 lb-ft
- **Drivetrain:** T84 three-speed manual, Dana-Spicer 18 two-speed transfer case
- **Axles:** Dana 25 front, full-floating Dana 23-2 rear
- **Propeller and bilge pump drive:** transfer case power take-off
- **Freeboard:** six inches
- **Fuel capacity/range on water:** 12 gallons/37 miles
- **Maximum speed:** 45 mph on land, 5.5 mph on water


Guildford Grammar School


Guildford Grammar School


Carlin found a boatyard manager who let him use their shop, where he fabricated a watertight canopy, false bow, extended propeller shaft and rudder, and added a keel. He attached a fuel tank beneath, and a freshwater tank, spare tire, and jerrycans occupied the aft deck. The rear seat was replaced with a wooden plank for sleeping, and the head was a bedpan stuffed under the seat. It was an environment that would send a sardine into claustrophobic convulsions.


Carlin during the initial construction, Maryland, 1947.


Guildford Grammar School


## Maritime Reunion


Elinore, meanwhile, wondering where her life was taking her and yearning for *something* exciting, couldn’t shake Ben’s pitch. That Aussie bloke’s hairbrained scheme might just fit the bill. She quit her job, moved back to the States, and wrote Ben a letter accepting his promise of adventure. He was ecstatic.


Guildford Grammar School


Initial testing, Annapolis, Maryland, circa 1947.


Guildford Grammar School


By 1947, the vessel was ready for a test run, which ended abruptly when a leaky axle seal nearly sent it to the bottom of the sea. The second attempt was cut short when Ben passed out from carbon monoxide poisoning, and a third found Ben and Elinore bobbing around the Atlantic for 10 days with a seized thrust bearing. Hoisted out of the drink by a freighter, they were deposited in Halifax, Nova Scotia. Elinore spent weeks prostrate on a wooden bunk vomiting into a tin cup (which was also used for morning tea), and though Ben offered to scrap the project, she refused.


Guildford Grammar School


Liberty Island, New York, 1948


Guildford Grammar School


Pier 11, Wall Street, New York, 1948


Guildford Grammar School


Sea trials in the Hudson River, circa 1948


Guildford Grammar School


## Departure


They dubbed the GPA *Half-Safe* , a moniker that had nothing to do with boats, Jeeps, or travel. It was borrowed from an Arrid deodorant ad of the time that stated, “Don’t be half-safe, be Arrid safe.” With a clear understanding that a GPA was never more than half safe on land or water, *Half-Safe* it was.


Guildford Grammar School


When the day arrived, July 19, 1950, without fanfare they fired up the flathead and set out from Halifax for the Azores. *Half-Safe* lacked documentation, and Elinore didn’t have a passport, but they did have food for six weeks, 880 gallons of fuel, 2300 hand-rolled cigarettes, and 2000 miles of open ocean ahead of them. What could go wrong in a 19-foot craft that could barely float?


> *No one was fooled, but nothing could be done to prevent our suicide.*
>
>
> *—Ben*


Guildford Grammar School


Guildford Grammar School


Guildford Grammar School


Guildford Grammar School


## Life Aboard


As we follow them into the Atlantic, we should note a number of potentially life-threatening mistakes: a forgotten fuel tank plug, a poorly attached life raft, an insufficiently sealed water tank. Ben and Elinore were capable, but the conditions they would endure were beyond comprehension. The weather began to freshen, and heat from the engine pushed cabin temperatures above the century mark. Considering both were chain smokers, existence in a 50-square-foot box bouncing around the ocean must have been dismal.


> *It would bore you if I tried to convey what Elinore was going through. Violently ill almost all the time, she sat day after night after day, the wheel in one hand and a busy pint mug in the other. For two-fisted stamina that girl took the cake.*
>
>
> *—Ben*


Deirdre Carlin


Deirdre Carlin


Ben listened to every rattle, creak, and rumble, and one morning the timbre hiccupped with a *thut thut thut* from the engine. The culprit was carbon buildup on the valves, so he pulled the head, cleaned it up, and they were once again underway. A day later they realized the water tank had been contaminated. With only a few bladder bags remaining, they were now on rations.


Guildford Grammar School


To reduce drag, Ben transferred fuel from the belly tank to a tow tank and jettisoned the refrigerator-sized appendage. The trick was to release all straps simultaneously—another well-intended plan foiled. Instead, Ben grabbed a knife and dove in, frantically slashing the remaining straps and then watching the tank slowly disappear into oblivion.


> *Had a breathless moment when Ben cut the straps… she didn’t go down immediately but listed so far to starboard that for a full minute it was touch & go whether we would go over.*
>
>
> *—Elinore*


## The Azores


Guildford Grammar School


Guildford Grammar School


Guildford Grammar School


Guildford Grammar School


After 32 days at sea, each suffering from exhaustion and dehydration, they arrived at the volcanic outcropping of Flores. Locals were aghast, struggling to comprehend how such a vessel could survive the Atlantic. Accepted as transient royalty, Ben and Elinore were presented with comforts bestowed on the most esteemed guests.


> *The hospitality of the island Portuguese is absolutely endless—one simply can refuse nothing and they keep heaping generosity upon generosity.*
>
>
> *—Ben*


Guildford Grammar School


Guildford Grammar School


Café Sport, Azores, 1950


José Henrique Azevedo


Their stay morphed into a months-long orgy of gluttonous indulgence. Hosted by a prominent family, Elinore led the life of a duchess while Ben made repairs and got hammered at Café Sport.


## Hell and High Water


Guildford Grammar School


Guildford Grammar School


Azores, 1950


Guildford Grammar School


Finally, the time came to shove off. They were advised that heavy seas were expected, but in Ben’s customarily belligerent manner, they pressed on. There is an old sailors’ saying that you will have bad luck and bad weather, but if they arrive together you are going to have a very bad day. Hell and high water were on the horizon.


Winds increased, swells reached 40 feet, and little could be done to control the vessel. One night the lifeboat slipped from its straps and was nearly lost. On another, the tow tank was ripped away and disappeared.


> *Another night hove to—7 ½ days in all. This is serious. Pitching very badly. Every 10 to 15 minutes we get a bad smack that comes right over the top—almost seems we are going to go over. I’d sell my soul for a bath, bacon & eggs, and a real bed.*
>
>
> *—Elinore*


The motor cut out again, and Ben stuck his head into the engine bay to repair a fuel line. Gas fumes filled the cabin and he was faced with two evils: Risk an explosion trying to get underway or get crushed by the swells and vanish into the depths. He pressed the ignition button.


Flames burst from the bow. “THIS IS IT… OUT!” He vaulted through the hatch expecting to find a hole in the foredeck, but all was intact. Back down he went, shoving Elinore’s emerging head into the cabin. Ben hit the ignition again, assuming the fumes had burned away. The little flathead fired up. They were afloat and alive but would soon be out of fuel. Ben tapped an SOS in Morse code, which was picked up by a passing freighter that located *Half-Safe* and provided fuel. After a week entombed in a hurricane, they would live to sail another day.


Guildford Grammar School


## North Africa, Gibraltar, and Steamy Affairs


Guildford Grammar School


Guildford Grammar School


Guildford Grammar School


Guildford Grammar School


Guildford Grammar School


Cape Juby and the Spanish Sahara


Northwest Africa at the time was controlled by Spain and France, and Ben and Elinore had been warned that landing at Cape Juby on the southern coast of Morocco would be a problem. There were no roads, and bandits roamed the region. After hiring an armed guide, they pointed the wheels north to the unknown. Although *Half-Safe* had four-wheel drive, it was anything but capable in technical terrain.


> *By nightfall we had covered no more than twelve miles, picking a way over endless areas of stony outcrops spiced with boulders. The going was murderously rough and by mid-morning we faced the first major obstacle—the five miles wide belt of dunes which I had been dreading.*
>
>
> *—Ben*


Since *Half-Safe* was neither car nor boat and lacked documentation, officials didn’t know what to do with them.


Gibraltar, 1950


Guildford Grammar School


> *Everyone here agog that we have no vehicle papers—they warn that we will not get across the border—and that Spaniards have a quaint habit of tossing people into jail and forgetting about them for 9 months or so… but because vehicle papers are beyond our means, will have to go at the frontier without.*
>
>
> *—Elinore*


A sympathetic officer in Gibraltar agreed to provide a triptyque for $20, which was $18 more than they had. After hawking equipment, they pulled together enough cash to legally enter Spain.


Flat broke, their existence became a rollercoaster ride. One week sleeping in a greasy shop and the next as guests in the palatial quarters of dignitaries such as Don Juan, Count of Barcelona. They scheduled public exhibitions, expecting their story would raise needed funds. Town folk came, but financial rewards were scant.


Guildford Grammar School


Guildford Grammar School


Guildford Grammar School


In August 1951, they crossed the English Channel for London, where the *Daily Express* had promised £500 for their story. That fell through. Perhaps more concerning than the lack of funds was that after months of submersion in saltwater, *Half-Safe* was falling apart.


> *Without warning she slumped on one knee and scraped to a halt on her nose.*
>
>
> *—Ben*


Guildford Grammar School


Guildford Grammar School


Ben decided England would be the best place for a full strip-down, but they were still destitute. His alcohol-induced insulting behavior toward Elinore had taken its toll, and when she got a job in London, he headed to Birmingham to work on *Half-Safe* .


Birmingham, England, 1952


Guildford Grammar School


England, 1954


Guildford Grammar School


England, 1955


Guildford Grammar School


Months turned to years, and Elinore became comfortable in her new city life, and the thought of climbing back into a floating sarcophagus was as nauseating as the month they had spent crossing the Atlantic. Meanwhile, a publisher offered Ben a £1000 advance to pen a book, which would pay for repairs and further the expedition. Elinore typed the manuscript and a female editor assigned to the project—who ended up in bed with Ben during their first session—made it suitable for print. Despite Ben’s shenanigans, Elinore decided she needed to finish what she started. If *Half-Safe* sailed from England, she would be on it.


Leaving Dover, England, 1955


Deirdre Carlin


Deirdre Carlin


English Channel, 1955


Deirdre Carlin


## London to Calcutta


Calais, France, 1955


Deirdre Carlin


France, 1955


Guildford Grammar School


Paris, 1955


Guildford Grammar School


In late April 1955, they left the island and began the journey through Europe, the Balkans, and the arid expanses of Iraq. Paranoid and battling with inner demons, Ben pushed *Half-Safe* , Elinore, and Frank Ringland (driving a support vehicle) to the brink of destruction. The Middle East was a continuum of bug-infested accommodation, cheap cigarettes, bottom-shelf vodka, and a road system in search of the 20th century. Desert heat brought cabin temperatures to 120 degrees, which required driving by night and sleeping by day. Pakistan, where Ben fired Ringland, was a blur, as was the 2000-mile crossing of India.


Iran, 1955


Guildford Grammar School


Iran, 1955


Guildford Grammar School


Pakistan, 1955


Guildford Grammar School


Considering India was where these lovebirds had met a decade earlier, their reunion that July with Calcutta was less than blissful. Ben greeted each day with a hangover and soon fell into a state of irritability and combativeness toward Elinore, until one day he slapped her. She was done.


Ben and Elinore in Calcutta, India, circa 1946


Guildford Grammar School


Ben in Calcutta, 1955


Guildford Grammar School


## Cigarettes and Amphetamines


In need of a co-driver, he placed an ad that read: “Man to take a year-long trip to New York… must be able to swim… not susceptible to seasickness… have mechanical experience and unlimited patience.” Barry Hanley, a 23-year-old draftsman, answered the call and agreed to meet *Half-Safe* in Akyab, Burma.


Ben Carlin with Barry Hanley, circa 1956


Guildford Grammar School


After slipping the wheels into the Bay of Bengal, Ben was on his own for the first time. It was not long before he began to miss his wife something terrible and penned pathetic letters of remorse in her absence.


> *For two pins I’d cable asking you to fly here, not because I’m short of crew…but because it’s just as painful living with you than without you.*
>
>
> *—Ben*


But Elinore hadn’t wasted any time getting on with life, and rumors filtered back of her whirlwind romance with a Texas paratrooper in Beirut. This drove Ben to madness. Sailing single-handed now, he lived on a diet of cigarettes and amphetamines. Little can be done for a man on the fast track to self-destruction.


Burma, 1956


Guildford Grammar School


Da Nang, Vietnam, 1956


Guildford Grammar School


After collecting Hanley, the two men looked north toward Thailand, where travel by land was said to be impossible. However, there is many a slip between the cup and the lip, and Ben learned of a track through the jungle. A local military commander pleaded they not attempt it, as it would require him to provide an escort. He apparently didn’t know Ben Carlin.


Saigon marked the midpoint of the circumnavigation. Ben’s map work had paid off, and following an orthodromic course to New York would lead directly to Hong Kong, the Sea of Japan, and Alaska.


Hong Kong, 1956


Guildford Grammar School


The Hong Kong Yacht Club received Ben like the King of England, and our wayward mariners were wined and dined and provided fuel. An inebriated fog and parade of geisha girls followed them through the Japanese archipelago, causing them to miss the weather window for a Pacific crossing. It was then that Hanley found a job and jumped ship.


Guildford Grammar School


Guildford Grammar School


Guildford Grammar School


Guildford Grammar School


## North Pacific


Boyé De Mente (L) and Ben Carlin (R).


Guildford Grammar School


Another ad led to Boyé De Mente, an American editor at the *Japan Times* who spoke Japanese, drank like a fish, and was quite the lady’s man. To flee copious numbers of heartbroken young ladies and their irate fathers, De Mente figured it was time to hit the road. Ben took an instant liking to him.


North Pacific, 1957


Guildford Grammar School


On June 12, 1957, *Half-Safe* entered the Sea of Okhotsk for the voyage to Shemya Island, the first of the Aleutians. The route put them just miles from the Russian military base at Sakhalin, where Japanese fishing boats routinely vanished in this Cold War black hole. Tensions were high as they sneaked by under the cloak of night. Heavy seas and mechanical issues brought back visions of the Atlantic, and Carlin’s Captain Bligh demeanor returned as a trough of darkness. De Mente realized he had made a big mistake.


Guildford Grammar School


One night a violent thud roused De Mente from the bunk; Ben had snagged a Japanese drift net and fouled the propeller. “This is going to be a chilly job … so the situation calls for a little fortifier,” Ben said, then chugged half a bottle of sake and stripped naked. At the end of the net was a Japanese fishing trawler, seamen shouting over the rail as Carlin lodged a knife between his teeth and jumped into the freezing water. Whether it was an alcohol-induced adrenaline rush or the superhuman act of a madman, he thrashed around and dove under the prop, only to pop up two shades bluer with each breath.


Eventually ensnared in the net, he was hauled onto the trawler like a frozen blue porpoise and taken inside. When he came to, Carlin fought off his captors and leaped over the rail into the water. Minutes passed before he surfaced and clawed his way onto *Half-Safe’s* deck. Days later they were still bobbing across the Pacific and late for a planned arrival on Shemya. The press again reported them as lost at sea, but Carlin’s wager with the devil was still on the table, and he was simply too damn stubborn to lose.


Shemya Island


Guildford Grammar School


A few days later, *Half-Safe* arrived in Shemya and newspapers hailed, “JAPAN-ALASKA TRIP COMPLETED BY JEEP.” After scavenging fuel from abandoned drums, they leapfrogged another 1400 miles to Homer, mainland North America. They made it, but De Mente had had enough and bailed out. “Ben was one of the most stubborn people I’ve ever met,” he later reflected.


Deirdre Carlin


## Bittersweet


With only 5000 easy miles to New York and the achievement of a dream, Carlin had beat insurmountable odds. By trip’s end, May 30, 1958, he and *Half-Safe* had covered 39,000 miles on land and 11,000 on water. The unobtainium had been obtained, and while this should have drawn elation, it sent him into a tailspin of depression. The thought of sinking back into a normal life was worse than that of vanishing at sea.


Guildford Grammar School


> *I faced returning to the jungle of life as a civilian, I would have to learn to be polite to painful numbies… lament over every tiny thing.*
>
>
> *—Ben*


One might ponder why this epic tale has been mostly forgotten. Sadly, Ben was a horrible promoter, a narcissist with a massive chip on his shoulder. He understood the power of the pen but was too damn cantankerous to give reporters the time of day. He yearned for acceptance, but deep down fought demons and the false pretense that he needed no one else. Elinore, the only person who believed in him, was gone, and he lived out his days alone and bitter, pitching movie scripts to anyone who would listen. There were no takers.


Gordon Bass


Love him or hate him, what Ben Carlin accomplished is truly inspiring and could probably never be repeated. Before his death in 1981, his last act in life was to leave his estate to his alma mater. If there is a happy ending to this story, it is that *Half-Safe* survived and has enjoyed a warm and dry retirement on display at the Guildford Grammar School outside Perth.
